newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS - Manila shares sink deeper, more drops seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Manila shares sink deeper, more drops seen.

text.p: Philippine shares sank to a new 17-month low on Monday and appeared headed for more declines as soaring domestic rates and unceasing fears of a Thailand-like economic slowdown again pounded the market, analysts said.
The market fell despite an announcement by Moody's Investors Service upgrading the long-term foreign currency debt and deposit ratings of 11 major domestic banks.
The 30-share index ended 2.6 percent lower on the day at 2,509.36 points.
It was the lowest the key barometer had fallen since December 19, 1995, and some analysts said they thought the market had yet to touch bottom.

"The momentum is still high on the downside. Maybe there are still more weaknesses expected," chief technical analyst Jonathan Ravelas of Asian Capital Equities said. "We think this thing will continue to persist."
Analysts said there might be some small rebounds ahead but said they had to be supported by strong volume for the market to pull out of its two-month-long slump.

Rising domestic rates, typified by Monday's jump of the Philipine 91-day Treasury bill rate to 11.166 percent from last week's 10.617 percent, and persistent concerns that the country was following the path of Thailand's economic downturn deepened the gloom, analysts said.
A possible rise in U.S. interest rates at Tuesday Federal Reserve Board meeting added to the wariness, they said.
"Comparisons made between the Philippines and Thailand continue to hound the local market," said Ardee Garcia, analyst at Diversified Securities.
All market sub-sectors reeled, with mining issues taking the biggest hit, falling 4.43 percent.
Foreign investors retreated in droves last month on fears that the property and banking problems that battered Thailand would be replicated in the Philippines.
Now, the Philippine peso has come under the same speculative attacks that recently hit the Thai baht.

So pervasive was the negative sentiment gripping the market that not even last week's announcement of a marked slowdown in the growth of country's trade deficit for the first quarter could bring cheer, analysts said.

"Investors are dwelling on the negative aspects," said Raul Ruiz, vice-president for research of Sun Hung Kai Securities Philippines. He said he expected foreign investors to stick to the sidelines for some time.
"We are going to see that for a long time the market will be tenative," he said.
